History:
• 43-year-old active female training for a marathon presents with right-dominant knee pain and audible clicking.  
• Onset: ~2 weeks ago after increasing running distance (now 7–8 mi runs).  
• Course: Pain begins ~20 min (~3 mi) into run; occasionally forces her to stop. Clicking noted during leg-extension/ab exercises at gym.  
• Associated symptoms: Single transient episode of mild knee swelling that resolved with ice; one episode of right-toe tingling post-run. No giving-way, locking, constant swelling, redness, fever, or limitation of daily walking/stairs.  
• Prior knee trauma: Bruise from ice-hockey fall a few months ago.  
• Relief/aggravating: Ice reduces swelling; rest stops pain; running and leg-extension provoke pain/clicking.  
• Review of other joints/limbs: No back pain, no small-joint swelling, no calf pain, no color/temperature change in legs.  

Past Medical History:
• Hyperopia; LASIK surgery.  
• Remote severe UTI (treated in ED).  
• No chronic illnesses reported.  
Allergies: Not documented.  
Medications:  
 – Ibuprofen 400 mg PRN (dose/route/frequency not fully documented)  
 – Aleve (naproxen) PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
 – Vitamin D supplement (dose not documented)  
 – Melatonin PRN (dose not documented)  
 – Xanax (alprazolam) occasional PRN (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
 – Occasional marijuana smoking.  

Physical Examination:
(tele-consultation; patient-reported findings)  
• Appearance: Alert, comfortable.  
• Right knee: Currently no visible swelling; full flexion and extension without locking; pain localized “middle then slightly to right” during activity; audible/subjective clicking with flexion-extension while exercising.  
• Left knee: Asymptomatic.  
• Gait, stairs, walking: No pain reported.  
• Calves/feet: No calf tenderness; no persistent edema; transient sock indentation after prolonged standing.  
• Neurovascular: Sensation normal; single past episode of toe tingling resolved.  
• Vitals and detailed musculoskeletal exam: Not recorded.

Impression:
Likely overuse/anterior knee pain syndrome—most consistent with patellofemoral pain syndrome (“runner’s knee”).  
Differential (consistent with transcript):  
1. Patellofemoral pain syndrome – activity-related anterior knee pain & clicking, onset with mileage increase.  
2. Patellar tendinopathy – overuse of extensor mechanism triggered by running/leg-extension.  
3. Degenerative/traumatic meniscal irritation – prior fall + clicking, although no locking/effusion.

Management Plan:
• Conservative therapy: Continue ice after activity; rest/modify training—reduce running distance/intensity until pain-free.  
• Pharmacologic: Prescribe stronger oral NSAID (agent and dosing unspecified in transcript) to be taken regularly with food; avoid concurrent ibuprofen/naproxen.  
• Referral: Issue referral to physiotherapy for comprehensive knee assessment, targeted strengthening, and biomechanical advice.  
• Contingency (“red flag”) advice: Seek urgent medical review if knee develops persistent swelling, heat, redness, high fever, feels unstable, or locks/unable to move.  
• Future evaluation: If symptoms persist despite physio, arrange in-clinic exam and consider imaging (e.g., MRI) to assess cartilage/meniscus/ligaments.

Patient Summary:
Middle-aged marathon trainee developed activity-related right knee pain and clicking after upping mileage two weeks ago. Exam is benign aside from mechanical symptoms. Presentation most consistent with patellofemoral overuse injury; plan is activity modification, NSAID course, and physiotherapy referral.

Key Takeaways:
• Rest and ice the knee after activity; avoid painful runs until symptoms settle.  
• Take the prescribed anti-inflammatory regularly with meals; do not combine with other NSAIDs.  
• Call back promptly if knee becomes swollen, red, hot, locked, or if fever or instability occurs.

Next Steps:
• Await physiotherapy appointment (referral sent today).  
• Follow up with primary care/clinic if no improvement after physio or within a few weeks.  
• Possible imaging (MRI) if mechanical symptoms or pain persist.
